objectives: Tell the difference between a slip and a real mistake.
Fix a mistake and try again.
Say sorry in a way that really helps.
Keep going after you get something wrong.
Ask a grown-up for help when a mistake is big.

sections.body:
A mistake is something you do that turns out wrong. You drop a cup. You write the wrong name. You say the wrong thing in a hurry.

Everybody makes mistakes. Grown-ups make them. Teachers make them. The people who look perfect are hiding theirs, not avoiding them.

Here is why mistakes happen. Your brain is still growing. It tries a new thing. Sometimes the try does not work. That is not a failure. That is a **try**.

Your brain learns by checking. It does something, sees what happened, and changes what it does next time. Without the wrong tries, it never learns what right looks like.

That is why babies wobble when they walk. Their legs are not broken. They are finding out how. A child who falls over and gets up is doing exactly what a body is supposed to do.

So mistakes are not the opposite of learning. Mistakes **are** learning, seen from the front.

The only real mistake is the one that stops you from trying again. A mistake you walk away from is just a bad day. A mistake you fix is a lesson you keep.
examples: I dropped the cup, but it did not break.
That was a try, and now I know how to do it.
sections.heading: Why everybody makes mistakes

sections.body:
Not all mistakes are the same size. It helps to know which kind you have.

A **slip** is a small one. You spelled a word wrong. You said your friend's name the wrong way. You tripped. Slips happen because you were busy. You fix a slip and move on.

A **real mistake** is bigger. You forgot somebody's birthday. You drew on somebody's paper. You said something unkind when you were angry. These need a sorry and a repair.

Some things cannot be undone. You broke a cup that belonged to somebody. You hurt a friend with your words. No sorry brings the cup back. But a sorry still matters, because it shows you now know better.

**Bigger mistakes** need an adult. If you broke something that costs a lot, if you hurt somebody, or if you are not sure what to do, tell a grown-up. Grown-ups can help you fix it, and sometimes they can talk to somebody for you.

Asking for help is not running away. It is the strongest thing a person can do.
examples: That was a slip. I will write it again.
I forgot your birthday. I am sorry.
I broke it. Please help me tell her.
sections.heading: Slips, mistakes, and the things you cannot undo

sections.body:
These are the words grown-ups use for mistakes. Knowing them helps you talk about yours.

A **mistake** is something you did that turned out wrong. It is not a bad person. It is a bad try.

To **try** means to have a go, even if it does not work. Trying is the bravest thing you can do.

To **fix** something means to make it right or better. Fixing a mistake can mean cleaning it, saying sorry, or doing it differently next time.

To **apologise** means to say sorry and show you understand what you did. A real apology has three parts.

A **slip** is a small mistake that happens because you were busy.

A **try** that failed is still a try. Grown-ups say *good try* when you did not finish. They mean it, and they mean it more than you think.

**Next time** is a useful phrase. It tells the other person that you have learned something and you will do it differently.
examples: Good try. You were very close.
Next time I will do it this way.
sections.heading: The words for mistakes

A small mistake that happens because you were busy or in a hurry.

sections.body:
When you make a mistake, four small steps help. Learn them and they work every time.

First, stop. Breathe. Your heart will be racing. Slow it down before you do anything else.

Next, notice. What exactly went wrong? Did you drop it, or did you knock it? Naming the mistake makes it smaller and easier to fix.

Then, fix what you can. Clean it up. Say sorry. Put it back. Draw it again properly.

After that, learn one thing. Not ten things. Just one. *I will hold it with two hands next time.*

And finally, try again. This is the step everybody forgets. The second try is the whole point.

Some mistakes need help. If you are not sure, or if somebody is upset, find a grown-up and say what happened. You will not get in trouble for telling the truth.
examples: Wait. Let me think for a second.
I will hold the cup with two hands next time.
Can you help me with this one?
sections.heading: What to do when you get it wrong
steps: Work out exactly what went wrong.
Learn one thing for next time.

sections.body:
Sorry means two different things in English. One is a quick word you say when you bump somebody. The other is a real apology. The real one helps much more.

A good apology has three parts. **Name it.** *I pushed you.* **Say why it was wrong.** *I was cross and I did not think.* **Say what you will do.** *I will walk instead of running.*

And then stop talking. Do not add *but*. *Sorry but you started it* is not an apology. It pushes the fault back.

Sometimes you are not sure you were wrong. Say so honestly and ask. *I think I was in your way. Was that me?* Sometimes the answer is yes and you say sorry. Sometimes it is no, and you both move on.

The hardest apology is the one where you were really, truly wrong and the other person is still angry. You say it anyway. You cannot make them feel better, and that is not your job. You can only be honest.

A good apology is not about making yourself feel good. It is about making the other person feel heard.
examples: I pushed you. I was cross and I did not think.
I will walk instead of running.
I think I was in your way. Was that me?
sections.heading: How to say sorry so it really helps

sections.body:
Some mistakes make you feel bad inside. That feeling has a name, and it is worth knowing.

**Guilt** is the feeling that you did something wrong and hurt somebody. Guilt is useful. It tells you to make it right. But guilt should not last for days.

**Shame** is the feeling that you are bad. Shame does not help anybody. Shame makes you hide and go quiet, and it makes it harder to learn.

Here is the difference. Guilt says: *that was a bad thing I did.* Shame says: *I am a bad thing.* Only the first one is true.

If you feel ashamed, talk to somebody you trust. A parent, a teacher, a friend. Say *I feel really bad about it.* Sometimes the feeling is bigger than the mistake, and a grown-up can help you put it down.

Then look for what you learned. Every mistake leaves a clue. That clue is the whole point of the mistake happening.

And here is the last thing. The person who made the mistake is not the whole story of you. You are not your worst moment. You are what you do after it.
examples: I feel bad about what I did.
That was a bad thing, but I am not a bad person.
I feel ashamed. Can we talk about it?
sections.heading: Feeling bad about it, and getting past that

item.summary: Everybody makes mistakes, and that is how people learn. After reading this you can spot a mistake, fix it, say sorry properly, and try again without feeling ashamed.
item.title: It's Okay to Make Mistakes
